title: A cross-species atlas platform for comparative neuroscience in teleost fish.
abstract: Uncovering general principles connecting neural circuits to behaviour requires comparative brain analyses across species. To advance these efforts, we developed a standardised workflow and a unified brain atlas platform for the quantitative comparison of neural structures between two teleost larvae, medaka (Oryzias latipes) and zebrafish (Danio rerio). Crucially, the platform seamlessly integrates user-generated image volumes, facilitating quantitative comparisons of anatomical, transcriptional, and functional data across species and laboratories. Utilising these integrated tools, we identified regional anatomical differences and differentially expressed genes between the species. We further demonstrated functionally distinct telencephalic regions in both species that exhibit divergent responses to social stimuli, suggesting an evolutionary divergence in social processing mechanisms. This web-based, interactive atlas platform promotes data exchange and knowledge sharing within the teleost community. Its scalable design permits effortless multi-group contributions, enabling expansion into a continuously growing, globally accessible database.

title: A systematic review of the spectrum of magnetic resonance imaging features of degenerative thoracic myelopathy.
abstract: Degenerative thoracic myelopathy (DTM) encompasses a range of degenerative pathologies associated with symptomatic spinal cord compression. Diagnosis is achieved through clinical history, examination, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A comprehensive review of the MRI features of DTM and their clinical significance is currently lacking. The objective was therefore to synthesise current evidence. A systematic review was performed adhering to PRISMA guidelines. MEDLINE and Embase were searched. Screening, data extraction and risk of bias assessments were performed in duplicate. A qualitative synthesis was conducted following the Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis (SWiM) guidelines. Of 7937 records, 59 papers studying 2940 patients satisfied inclusion criteria, including one cross-sectional and 58 cohort studies. DTM was most common in the lower thoracic spine (62.5%, 880/1409), with a roughly equal prevalence in the upper (18.2%, 256/1409) and middle regions (19.4%, 273/1409). Ossification of the ligamentum flavum (OLF) was the most common pathology (71.4%, 2065/2893), followed by intervertebral disc herniation (20.1%, 582/2893) and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) (19.7%, 569/2893). Measurements of spinal canal compromise were described in 55.5% of patients (1631/2940) and spinal cord signal change in 30.0% (881/2940). Spinal canal compromise, spinal cord signal change, OLF, OPLL and multilevel disease were associated with greater DTM severity and poorer functional recovery. Ligamentous pathologies are significantly more prevalent than disc related pathologies in the DTM literature. Spinal cord signal change and extent of spinal canal compromise correlate with clinical outcomes. Standardisation of terminology for imaging features and study design are required to improve future research.

title: Developing a microsimulation model of Alzheimer's disease for the evaluation of disease modifying therapies.
abstract: Clinical trials of amyloid-targeting therapies (ATTs) for Alzheimer's Disease (AD) showed slowing of decline in continuous cognitive and functional outcomes over eighteen months of follow-up. Existing simulation models used to extrapolate these results do not account for the distinct but correlated trajectories of cognitive and functional decline, limiting their accuracy in evaluating ATT effects on both domains. We developed an AD microsimulation model using an amyloid-positive memory clinic population that can translate slowed cognitive decline into effects on clinical functional independence stages. The model contained stages of mild cognitive impairment (MCI), community dementia, institutionalisation, and death. The transitions from MCI to dementia and from dementia to institutionalisation or death were related to Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) measurements through statistical joint models. Model validation showed that observed and predicted cumulative incidence curves overlapped for all stage transitions, indicating an accurate description of time in each stage. An untreated cohort starting with MCI had a mean duration of MCI, mild, moderate and severe community dementia, and institutionalisation of 3.3, 2.3, 1.6, 1.1, and 1.7 years, respectively, totalling 10.0 years. When ATTs slowed MMSE decline by 30% during MCI and mild dementia (community dementia with an MMSE above 20), the duration of MCI and mild dementia was prolonged by 0.4 and 1.0 years, respectively, and institutionalisation was delayed by 1.1 year. The time institutionalised remained similar. Our AD microsimulation model can translate ATT effects on cognition into effects on functional independence and can be used to assess the cost-effectiveness of new therapies.

title: Dose-Response Effects of Exercise Training on Circulating Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF): A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
abstract: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is involved in neuroplasticity, but circulating BDNF is not a validated surrogate for brain BDNF. We synthesised randomised controlled trials comparing chronic exercise with a non-exercising control. Change-score standardised mean differences (Hedges' g) were pooled using restricted maximum likelihood and Hartung-Knapp inference. The analysis included 48 trials, 56 exercise-versus-control comparisons and 2361 unique participants. Shared control sample sizes were apportioned across comparisons, with trial-cluster robust sensitivity analyses. Exercise increased circulating BDNF on average (g = 0.41, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.57; p < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 67.0%; 95% prediction interval - 0.54 to 1.36). Serum-based comparisons yielded g = 0.27 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.44) and plasma-based comparisons g = 0.69 (0.37 to 1.00); the matrix moderator was significant in the primary analysis (p = 0.017) but not under trial-cluster robust inference (p = 0.065). Population, modality and intervention duration were not significant primary moderators. In the joint dose model (33 comparisons from 29 trials), neither total prescribed exercise volume (β = 0.037 per 1000 min, p = 0.614) nor vigorous versus moderate intensity (β = - 0.190, p = 0.361) was associated with the BDNF effect. Weekly-volume and quadratic analyses did not establish a dose-response relationship. The overall effect remained positive after restricting sampling to approximately ≥ 24 h after exercise (g = 0.35, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.58). Egger's test indicated small-study effects (p = 0.011). The certainty of evidence was very low. Chronic exercise is associated with an average increase in circulating BDNF, but heterogeneity, methodological limitations and uncertain moderator effects prevent a biomarker-specific exercise prescription or an inference of increased central BDNF. PROSPERO registration: CRD420261448624.

title: The role of astrocytes in the temporoammonic pathway: masticatory behavior as a neuroprotective strategy against age-related cognitive decline.
authors: de Siqueira Mendes Fabíola de Carvalho Chaves
Brites Dora Maria Tuna de Oliveira
abstract: Astrocytes undergo phenotypic changes with aging, contributing to neurodegenerative diseases and cognitive impairments in later life. The temporoammonic (TA) pathway terminates at the stratum lacunosum-moleculare (SLM) of the CA1 region, where astrocytic support is crucial for synaptic plasticity and information processing related to spatial learning and memory. This study tested the hypothesis that age-related morphological changes in astrocytes of the SLM affect cognitive performance and we explored whether masticatory activity modulates these changes. Young (6 months) and aged (18 months) female Swiss albino mice were subjected to three distinct masticatory regimens: a hard diet (HD), HD followed by a soft diet (HD/SD), or HD followed by SD and a return to HD (HD/SD/HD). Cognitive performance was assessed using the Morris Water Maze (MWM), with learning rates calculated from escape latencies throughout five days of trials. After behavioral testing, the mice were culled and immunohistochemical analysis of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) expression was performed. 3D reconstructions of astrocytes within the SLM were generated and analyzed. Hierarchical clustering identified distinct astrocyte morphotypes, revealing a significant age-related shift from high-complexity astrocytes (AST1) toward lower-complexity subtypes (AST2 and AST3). In the AST1 phenotype, aging did not significantly alter astrocytic complexity in animals maintained under normal masticatory conditions (HD group) in the dorsal region, then, AST1 may represent a more stable and aging-driven astrocytic phenotype, with limited sensitivity to masticatory modulation during advanced aging. Therefore, in AST2 of HD group, aged animals exhibited greater complexity compared to young animals, suggesting the occurrence of adaptive or compensatory astroglial remodeling during physiological aging. Behavioral analysis showed an age-dependent reduction in learning performance in the HD group, where 18 M mice exhibited a significantly lower contrast index than 6 M old mice on day 4 of the Morris Water Maze task. These findings highlight that morphological changes in astrocytes within the dorsal SLM may contribute to age-related alterations in hippocampus-dependent learning. Overall, maintaining proper mastication may be an effective approach to maintain astrocytic integrity during aging and preserve hippocampus-dependent cognitive function, particularly in older individuals.

title: Multimodal analysis reveals asynchronous aging dynamics between endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer and endometriosis patients.
abstract: The malignant transformation of endometriosis into endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer (EAOC) is still of great interest among researchers. Despite the shared inflammatory and hormonal drivers, the cellular aging dynamics differentiating these two pathologies remain elusive. This study aimed to quantify biological aging using DNA methylation status and telomere length to identify distinct signatures associated with disease progression. We conducted a comparative analysis of multiple aging-related biomarkers in blood, including biological age, telomere length, and DNA methylation status, as well as specific longevity markers, across cohorts of age-matched patients with endometriosis and EAOC, compared with unaffected controls. Precision assessment utilized machine learning models to determine biological age deviation and methylation levels at specific CpG sites. Finally, the study employs a Random Forest machine learning classifier to assess the discriminative power of gene signatures, complemented by Gene Ontology enrichment. Our analysis revealed a profound divergence in biological aging trajectories. Patients with endometriosis exhibited significant age acceleration (+ 16.92%) and maintained telomeres that were significantly longer (13.18 ± 0.46 kbp). Conversely, EAOC patients displayed a biologically younger profile compared to their chronological age (- 14.64%). These patients also demonstrated significant telomeric attrition (12.45 ± 0.72 kbp; p < 0.001), reflecting their extensive mitotic history and the rapid turnover of malignant cells. Age-related methylation was the most robust marker, distinguishing the groups with high statistical significance. This study provides novel evidence that the transition from endometriosis to EAOC involves a fundamental shift in biological age and in telomere dynamics. Identifying these divergent aging signatures offers a powerful tool for precision oncology, enabling the development of predictive models to identify patients at high risk of malignant transformation and facilitating personalized interceptive strategies based on biological, rather than chronological age.

title: The macrophage as a neuroimmune sensor and effector: neural control of inflammation across tissues and disease.
journal: Inflammation research : official journal of the European Histamine Research Society ... [et al.]
abstract: Once viewed mainly as scavengers of innate immunity, macrophages are now recognized as constitutive partners of the nervous system. In neural tissue their identity is instructed by neurons and glia, and in turn they shape neural function - pruning synapses, tuning neuronal excitability, and executing the autonomic commands that restrain inflammation. Here we advance a mechanistic model built on three principles: that neural and glial signals specify macrophage identity on a shared myeloid template; that the macrophage is a bidirectional sensor-effector node within autonomic reflex arcs, both relaying neural output and generating the cytokine signals that afferent nerves detect; and that this sensor-effector arc is modular, recurring across brain, spleen, gut, heart, and adipose tissue. We give particular attention to the afferent limb of the inflammatory reflex, which now extends beyond the vagus to nociceptors and to the carotid body, an arterial chemoreceptor that senses circulating inflammatory signals and recruits a sympathetic anti-inflammatory pathway, and to the stress-responsive circuitry through which sympathetic outflow drives myelopoiesis, neuroinflammation, and sickness behavior. We then turn to disease, in which macrophage function is altered by a diseased or aged niche in neurodegeneration, chronic pain, gut-brain disorders, and metabolic disease. Whether the neuroimmune circuits described here are themselves disrupted in these conditions, rather than merely coexisting with them, is largely untested, and we outline what such evidence would require. We close by arguing that tuning these circuits, rather than broadly suppressing macrophage activity, is the more plausible therapeutic goal.

title: Spatiotemporally resolved single-nucleus transcriptomics reveals cellular and regional vulnerability in the midbrain in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is clinically and biologically heterogeneous, and ethnic differences may influence its pathogenesis. However, single-nucleus transcriptomic data from East Asian populations remain limited. Here, we present a spatially resolved single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of the human substantia nigra (SN) across the PD continuum, control, incidental Lewy body disease (iLBD), and advanced PD, in pathologically confirmed Korean individuals. Our integrative analysis revealed early α-synuclein aggregation in the ventrolateral SN, subtype-selective vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons, and relative preservation of the dorsomedial SN and ventral tegmental area. Trajectory and gene regulatory network analyses of astrocytes and microglia revealed spatiotemporally distinct, disease-associated glial responses, each driven by divergent molecular programs. We also identified two transcriptionally distinct vascular spatial clusters that exhibited differential vulnerability and remodeling. Spatial ligand-receptor analysis of α-synuclein-positive regions revealed intercellular signaling events associated with early pathology, including extracellular matrix remodeling and synaptic adhesion, which were prominent in the iLBD but largely diminished in advanced PD. Integration with PD genome-wide association studies using MAGMA demonstrated differential coupling between genetic risk, spatially resolved cell-state programs, and pseudotime-inferred microglial dynamics across ancestries. This study provides the first high-resolution, spatially mapped single-nucleus transcriptomic resource from an East Asian PD cohort, illuminating early perturbations in the midbrain intercellular and microenvironment that may underlie selective dopaminergic vulnerability and guide the development of ancestry-informed therapeutic strategies.

title: Learning to become an osteopath in Italy: a qualitative study of first-year students in a newly established university programme.
abstract: To explore how first-year undergraduate osteopathy students construct their emerging professional identity during early education within the first Italian university-based osteopathy degree programme, with particular attention to the role of embodied learning, early clinical exposure, and institutional uncertainty. A qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. A newly established undergraduate osteopathy degree programme at the University of Verona, Italy. A total of 17 first-year osteopathy students were involved through purposive sampling to capture variation in age, gender and educational background. Students' meaning-making of emerging professional identity, with particular attention to embodied learning, early clinical exposure, relational recognition, and institutional uncertainty. Four themes were developed from the analysis. (1) "Entering an undefined profession: between privilege and uncertainty", where students experienced enrolment as meaningful while navigating an evolving institutional context. (2) "Learning through the body: from studying osteopathy to feeling like an osteopath", highlighting the gap between theoretical knowledge and embodied confidence. (3) "The internship: legitimacy, exposure and vulnerability", where clinical encounters were described as simultaneously supporting and challenging students' emerging sense of professional legitimacy. (4) "Being an osteopath-in-training: a provisional, fragile and relational identity", illustrating how participants described negotiating their emerging professional identity through interaction, recognition, and institutional uncertainty. Early professional identity in a newly established osteopathy programme was experienced as provisional, embodied, and relational. Participants reported their early professional identity as closely linked not only to clinical learning, but also to the institutional conditions in which they learned, practised, and began to see themselves as future professionals. Our findings suggest that participants experienced institutional uncertainty not merely as a contextual challenge but as an important dimension of how they made sense of their developing competencies, legitimacy and recognition during early professional education. Recognising and supporting these processes may strengthen educational practice in health professions that are newly integrated into higher education, as well as in other evolving academic contexts.

title: Instrumented assessment of joint neuromechanics in upper motor neuron syndrome: a systematic review of methods, reliability, validity, and clinical relevance.
abstract: Instrumented neuromechanical assessment (I-NMA) is a promising method for quantifying joint neuromechanics in upper motor neuron syndrome (UMNS), using controlled joint manipulation such as stretch- or continuous perturbations. Compared to traditional clinical assessments, I-NMA can provide improved insight by better separating neural and mechanical contributions and increasing objectivity. However, I-NMA has not yet found its way into clinical practice, possibly due to methodological shortcomings. This systematic review analyzed 74 studies on I-NMA using controlled perturbation in UMNS, examining experimental protocols, input-output analyses to quantify neuromechanical outcome parameters, and their reliability and validity. Most studies employed only single-joint (n=64 studies) assessments, solely under passive conditions (n=63), which overlook clinically relevant aspects such as multi-joint interactions and active control. Among neuromechanical parameters, joint stiffness and reflexive resistance were quantified most, whereas joint dampingand intrinsic neural drive contributions remained underrepresented. Four main input-output analysis methods were recognized: System Quantification (n=55), System Modeling (n=12), and System Identification via impulse (IRF, n=7), or frequency response functions (FRF, n=6). The first quantified passive stiffness during a slow joint stretch and reflexive resistance during a fast stretch. The latter three quantified neuromechanical parameters by fitting models, comprising time-delayed reflex components and intrinsic joint stiffness and damping, either directly using input-output data (System Modeling) or via initial nonparametric IRF or FRF estimation. The reliability of quantified parameters showed substantial room for improvement, especially in the minimal detectable change, ranging from 20% to 947% of the parameter value across analyses. I-NMA outcome measures showed stronger validity when assessed against expected UMNS-healthy differences than when assessed against clinical scales. Future I-NMA development may benefit from improved reliability through protocol consistency and optimized analysis, stronger evidence for the valid separation of neural and mechanical constructs, and enhanced clinical relevance by using active and passive assessments, capturing both paresis and hyperresistance.

title: Performance and response time in emotion recognition and mentalizing measures in patients with schizophrenia.
abstract: Schizophrenia is associated with marked impairments in social cognition, particularly in emotion recognition and mentalizing. Although these deficits have been extensively documented, most studies rely on static, highly controlled measures and focus primarily on accuracy-based outcomes, thereby limiting ecological validity. This study aimed to examine performance and response times across static and dynamic social-cognitive measures in patients with schizophrenia compared to healthy controls, and to investigate the effects of speed instructions on emotion recognition performance. In a sample of patients with schizophrenia (n = 90) and matched healthy controls (n = 100), we evaluated social cognition through two validated measures: the Penn Emotion Recognition Test (ER-40) for emotion recognition and the Movie for the Assessment of Social Cognition (MASC) for mentalizing, respectively. Performance and response times were the main outcome variables. Patients showed worse performance and longer response times than controls on the ER-40 and MASC measures. Across the entire sample, there was a statistically significant inverse association between response time and the rate of correct answers in both ER-40 and MASC measures. Speed instructions in the ER-40 did not influence performance or response times in either group. In the MASC, patients exhibited more mentalizing errors than controls. Additionally, patients identified anger more quickly than fear or sadness, a pattern not observed in the healthy control group. Integrating accuracy and response time provides a comprehensive characterization of social-cognitive deficits in patients with schizophrenia. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating response time and dynamic measures to enhance the ecological validity of social-cognitive assessment and suggest that future rehabilitation programs may benefit from addressing both accuracy and response speed in emotion recognition and mentalizing domains.

title: Co-production and co-evaluation of public health communication of invasive Group A Streptococcal infection (iGAS) for people experiencing homelessness and people who inject drugs.
abstract: Invasive group A streptococcal (iGAS) disease is a rare but serious bacterial infection affecting a broad cross-section of people. Public health advice is routinely provided to close contacts of iGAS cases to encourage early presentation to medical facilities, given the elevated risk of secondary transmission. Despite being at heightened risk, people experiencing homelessness (PEH) and people who inject drugs (PWID) have not been involved in developing the pre-existing public health materials, and therefore they may not be accessible, understandable, or actionable for these groups. Coproduction is an approach in which people with lived experience work in partnership with researchers, in this case, to design and evaluate interventions intended for their use. This project (1) explored the experiences and communication needs of PEH and PWID; (2) coproduced iGAS factsheets with PEH and PWID; and (3) evaluated whether the coproduced materials were accessible, understandable, non-stigmatising, and actionable. We used the Agile Co-production and Evaluation (ACE) framework to embed coproduction throughout the development and evaluation of iGAS public health materials, recognising the need for approaches tailored to the contexts and constraints faced by PEH and PWID. A multidisciplinary steering group including public health professionals, service providers, and researchers guided the study. The protocol was pre-registered (OSF: z4268) and the study is reported in accordance with GRIPP2 long-form guidelines for public involvement. Coproduction activities informed factsheet modifications incorporating simplified language, visual cues, and content relevant to PEH and PWID. Coproducers described the new factsheet as eye-catching, easy to read, and person-centred whereas the original version was viewed as having limited relevance. In the evaluation survey, 32/39 responders preferred the coproduced factsheet, which was rated higher for readability and clarity. Symptoms of iGAS were correctly identified and responders reported they would follow the advice. Coproduction can improve the design and evaluation of public health advice for underserved groups. Using the ACE framework, coproduced materials were clearer, more actionable, and better aligned with the needs of PEH and PWID. The process also identified practical considerations for health protection teams and future incident settings.

title: Prefrontal dysfunction and impulsive decision-making in female methamphetamine use disorder: a fNIRS study.
abstract: Heightened preference for immediate over delayed rewards is a well-established feature of substance use disorders, yet the neural basis of this tendency in women with methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) remains insufficiently characterized. Delay discounting provides a useful behavioral index of impulsive decision-making, and convergent evidence implicates prefrontal valuation and control systems in addiction-related choice abnormalities. Twenty-five women with MUD and 25 healthy women completed an intertemporal decision-making task under gain and loss frames. Delay discounting rates were estimated using the hyperbolic discounting parameter (k). Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to assess oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO) responses in predefined prefrontal regions of interest, with a focus on the medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Trait impulsivity/reinforcement sensitivity was assessed using the BIS/BAS scales. Behavioral discounting was analyzed using a linear mixed model, and neural indices were analyzed using repeated-measures ANCOVAs with age as a covariate and FDR correction across ROIs. Compared with healthy controls, women with MUD showed significantly steeper delay discounting, indicating a stronger preference for immediate outcomes. They also exhibited lower HbO responses in the right mOFC and left DLPFC during task performance, as well as reduced task-related HbO change in the right DLPFC. Lower right mOFC mean task-window HbO was associated with higher BIS/BAS composite scores. No robust Group × Frame interaction was observed for behavioral discounting. Women with MUD showed altered intertemporal choice and reduced prefrontal hemodynamic responses in regions implicated in value evaluation and cognitive control. These findings support the relevance of prefrontal dysfunction to impulsive decision-making in female MUD while also indicating that framing-related effects should be interpreted cautiously. The study extends the limited literature on women with MUD and supports the use of fNIRS to examine prefrontal mechanisms of addiction-related decision-making. Not applicable.

title: Early neurological deterioration after endovascular treatment in acute ischemic stroke with large vessel occlusion.
abstract: This study aimed to explore the occurrence, identify independent predictors, and assess the clinical implications of END following EVT in individuals with acute LVO. Participants were enrolled from the ANGEL-ACT registry. END was characterized by a rise of ≥ 4 points in the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score from baseline to 24 h post-EVT. We conducted logistic regression analyses to pinpoint independent predictors of END. Among the 1557 patients included in the study, the occurrence of END stood at 9.8%. Factors independently associated with END included an admission NIHSS (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 4.067, 95% CI 2.513 to 6.582, p < 0.0001), an admission neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) exceeding 5 (aOR = 1.811, 95% CI 1.246 to 2.632, p = 0.0018), the use of general anesthesia (GA) (aOR = 0.474, 95% CI 0.330 to 0.682, p < 0.0001), longer procedure duration (aOR = 5.500, 95% CI 1.45 to 20.871, p = 0.0122), and more than three retrieval attempts (aOR = 1.294, 95% CI 1.177 to 1.422, p < 0.0001). END manifested in 9.8% of patients undergoing endovascular therapy (EVT) for acute large vessel occlusion (LVO). This investigation highlights various independent predictors of END, providing valuable insights for daily clinical practice aimed at enhancing the effectiveness of intravascular thrombectomy. URL: https://www. gov ; Unique identifier: NCT03370939; registration date: 11th November 2017.

title: A subset of SLC2A1 missense variants interfere with GLUT1 trafficking in human brain endothelial cells.
abstract: Glucose transporter type 1 (GLUT1), encoded by the SLC2A1 gene, mediates basal glucose uptake and is essential for brain energy homeostasis. Genetic variants in SLC2A1 cause GLUT1 Deficiency Syndrome (GLUT1 DS), a rare neurometabolic disorder characterized by impaired glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier and encompassing a wide and expanding phenotypic spectrum. Despite the fact that a high proportion of reported pathogenic SLC2A1 variants are missense, their effects on GLUT1 cellular biology remain incompletely understood, and the relative contribution of altered transport, protein stability, and intracellular trafficking has not been fully defined. Eight SLC2A1 missense variants were selected and mutants were generated by site-directed mutagenesis of GLUT1-EGFP encoding plasmid. Subcellular localization and trafficking were investigated by using confocal microscopy and quantitative colocalization analysis in human brain endothelial (hCMEC/D3) and HeLa cells, also in response to changes in extracellular glucose availability; protein content in response to autophagy perturbation was evaluated by western blotting; protein degradation rate was assessed through cycloheximide chase assays. We found that four of the selected variants were associated with altered GLUT1 distribution and responsiveness to extracellular glucose availability, promoting intracellular retention, with most of them showing marked association to lysosome-related compartments (N34S, R126L and Q283R). Our study identifies variant-associated differences in GLUT1 intracellular distribution in a subset of pathogenic SLC2A1 missense variants, with increased lysosomal targeting representing a recurrent cellular fate. These findings provide insights into variant-associated differences in GLUT1 cellular behaviour and highlight intracellular trafficking analysis as a complementary approach to transport-based functional assays for investigating GLUT1 biology. Further studies integrating cellular phenotypes with patient-derived models, biochemical and clinical data will be required to determine how the observed trafficking alterations relate to disease biology and clinical presentation.

title: EXPRESS: Brain on fire: Why intracerebral hemorrhage requires a firefighting strategy beyond single therapeutic targets.
journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism
abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains the most lethal form of stroke and lacks an established neuroprotective therapy. Secondary injury after ICH reflects interacting processes, including hematoma expansion, hemolysis-derived toxicity, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, perihematomal edema, oxidative stress, and regulated cell death. Although mechanistic single-target studies remain essential for defining biological relevance, treatment windows, target engagement, and safety, ICH is unlikely to be adequately addressed by any one intervention alone. Using the analogy of a "fire in the brain," this perspective proposes a coordinated, time-sensitive firefighting framework: Rapid blood-pressure management and hemostatic reversal can limit continued bleeding. Hematoma evacuation can remove biological fuel in selected patients. Interventions targeting lipid peroxidation and oxidative injury may limit secondary combustion. Inflammation- and edema-directed therapies may contain harmful heat. Enhancement of endogenous hematoma clearance may promote resolution and repair. Imaging and biomarkers can support phenotyping, monitoring, and treatment selection. Emerging signals from care bundle, minimally invasive evacuation, and experimental combination studies support the testing of staged, biologically rational add-on strategies rather than fixed therapeutic cocktails. The goal is not to deploy all the tools at once, but to match appropriate interventions to the evolving biology, phenotype, timing, feasibility, and care context of each hemorrhage.

title: Microbial serotonin signalling axes in irritable bowel syndrome: integrative molecular crosstalk among enterochromaffin cells, gut microbiota, neuroimmune circuits, and precision therapeutic engineering.
abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common, often disabling disorder of gut-brain interaction whose molecular basis remains incompletely defined, leaving diagnosis largely symptom-based and treatment largely non-mechanistic. We argue that the serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; hereafter 5-HT, the primary term used throughout, with "serotonin" retained in less technical contexts) signalling axis-positioned at the interface of the gut microbiota, enterochromaffin (EC) cells, enteric neurons, and the mucosal immune system-is a central, unifying integrator of IBS pathophysiology, and that reframing IBS around this axis offers a route toward mechanism-based subtyping and therapy. We first synthesise how microbiota-driven tryptophan metabolism, short-chain fatty acid and secondary bile acid signalling, and epigenetic regulation of tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) shape EC-cell serotonin output, before examining the neuroimmune consequences of dysregulated serotonin secretion-mast cell activation, macrophage polarisation, neurogenic inflammation-and the microbiota-serotonin-gut-brain connectome linking vagal afferent signalling, blood-brain barrier permeability, and central neurotransmitter networks. We then discuss molecular stratification of IBS subtypes through serotonergic endotyping-incorporating SLC6A4 and TPH1 polymorphisms, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics-and critically evaluate next-generation therapeutic strategies, including engineered probiotic chassis, CRISPR-mediated microbial editing, and AI-guided nanomedicine, distinguishing proof-of-concept findings from clinically validated approaches. We conclude that reconceptualising IBS as a disorder of disrupted microbial serotonergic ecosystems, rather than a purely symptom-defined syndrome, offers a coherent and testable framework for biomarker discovery and precision, mechanism-directed therapy, while highlighting the causal-directionality and clinical-translation gaps that must be closed before this framework can be applied at the bedside.

title: Entrainment of prefrontal theta synchrony increases interbrain coupling and enhances social interaction in mouse models of autism.
abstract: Social interaction requires the integration of information about self, other, and shared context. One of the proposed mechanisms supporting this coordination is interbrain synchrony - correlated neural activity between interacting individuals - yet its role in shaping social behavior remains unresolved. Here, we show that theta band synchrony in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is closely linked to social interaction in mice and often precedes its onset. In male Shank2 mutant mice, a genetic model of social dysfunction, mPFC interbrain synchrony was diminished, along with a reduced population of mPFC neurons encoding multiple dimensions of social information. Optogenetic entrainment of theta synchrony was accompanied by increased interbrain coupling and social interaction in male Shank2-/- and Tbr1+/K228E mutant mice, two well-established genetic models of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). These findings identify prefrontal theta synchrony as a neural substrate that supports social behavior and provide a framework for understanding how coordinated neural activity across brains contributes to social interaction.

title: Dummy template-assisted chiral molecularly imprinted polymer-capillary electrochromatography with synergistic functional monomers for the enantioseparation of multiple β-blockers.
abstract: Conventional chiral molecularly imprinted polymers (CMIPs) are constrained by the "single template-single target" recognition mode, which limits their chiral recognition spectrum. To address this issue, this study exploited the common core scaffold of β-blockers as the entry point. (S)-1-(Isopropylamino)-3-phenoxy-2-propanol (S-IPP), a byproduct of metoprolol production, was selected as a dummy template, with 4-vinylpyridine and itaconic acid synergistically employed as dual functional monomers. A dummy template-based CMIPs monolithic capillary column (DT-CMIPs@capillary) was directly prepared via in situ polymerization within the capillary, and a DT-CMIPs-CEC enantioseparation system was subsequently established. Through systematic optimization of the monolithic column preparation conditions and CEC separation parameters, enantioseparation of eight β-blockers was successfully achieved to varying degrees, with resolution values (RS) ranging from 0.53 to 9.83 and following a clear gradient that correlated with the structural similarity of each analyte to the dummy template. This gradient was highly correlated with the structural similarity of each drug molecule, thereby validating the effectiveness of the dummy template strategy in broadening the recognition spectrum. Furthermore, static adsorption experiments were conducted to determine the selectivity factor (SF), and the correlation between SF and RS was systematically analyzed. On this basis, a preliminary chiral recognition mechanism model was proposed from three aspects: thermodynamic selectivity, kinetic mass transfer, and structural matching integrity. This study transforms the industrial byproduct S-IPP into a functional recognition element, providing a cost-effective and broad-spectrum platform for the chiral analysis of β-blocker drugs, while also offering theoretical insights and experimental reference for the design of dummy template-based imprinted materials.

title: Dysglycemia during neonatal encephalopathy and early school-age neurodevelopmental outcomes.
abstract: To assess the relationship between neonatal dysglycemia and early school-age neurodevelopmental outcomes after neonatal encephalopathy. A prospective cohort born at 36 weeks or more of gestation with neonatal encephalopathy underwent continuous glucose monitoring, neonatal magnetic resonance imaging, and neurodevelopmental assessments at 5 years 6 months (5 months). Linear regression analyses assessed the relationship between glucose (minimum, maximum thresholds of 8-13 mmol/l, and SD) and neurodevelopmental outcomes (Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition and Child Behavior Checklist composite scores), adjusting for sex, neonatal brain injury severity, and parental education. Of 61 newborn infants (40 males), three had mild, 55 had moderate, and three had severe encephalopathy. Maximum glucose greater than 13 mmol/L was associated with a 17.4-point lower full-scale IQ (p = 0.043), 17.4 lower Fluid Reasoning Index (p = 0.037), and 13.5 lower Processing Speed Index (p = 0.032). Higher SD of glucose was associated with a 5.0-point lower Fluid Reasoning Index (p = 0.038). Significance was lost after adjusting for neonatal brain injury and/or paternal education. No associations were found between minimum glucose and 5- to 6-year outcomes (p > 0.456). In the era of therapeutic hypothermia, hyperglycemia and increased glucose variability during the first few days of life are associated with worse neurodevelopmental outcomes at early school-age in survivors of neonatal encephalopathy. These associations could be explained by neonatal brain injury and/or paternal education.

title: MDM2/X mediates reduced apoptosis in the plateau zokor: a mechanism of high-altitude adaptation.
journal: Journal of Zhejiang University. Science. B
abstract: Murine double minute 2 (MDM2) and murine double minute 4 (MDMX) are critical for the regulation of tumor protein 53 (p53) function and apoptosis. This study compares the Mdm2/x gene sequences and functional variations of subterranean zokors from the High Plateau and the Loess Plateau. The findings reveal the molecular mechanisms by which Mdm2/x variations drive adaptation to extremely high-altitude conditions-including low oxygen, cold temperatures, and perpetual darkness in underground environments. We cloned and analyzed Mdm2/x sequences from two distinct ecological groups of subterranean rodents, Myospalax baileyi (plateau zokor) and Myospalax cansus (Gansu zokor), and reconstructed phylogenetic trees for a series of subterranean rodents and mammals, as well as the aboveground laboratory rat and humans. We found that MDM2/X in M. baileyi and M. cansus are involved in the p53-dependent low apoptosis rate, and the variations of phosphorylation sites at the C-terminus of MDM2 contribute to upregulation of p53 transcription and protein expression. We propose that gene evolutionary mechanisms enable survival under these severe combined pressures, and believe that our findings provide critical insight into how genetic modifications drive physiological resilience in Earth's most challenging ecosystems.

title: Interleukin-31 Induces Itch-Related Responses with Precursor Behaviors in Mice and Its Suppression by the Dopamine D2/D3 Receptor Agonist Ropinirole.
abstract: Recent research has revealed that human itch manifests in a variety of distinct phenotypes, such as muzumuzu (creepy-crawly itch, a bit like tickling). We have also demonstrated that scratching behaviors induced by pruritogens in mice are sometimes preceded by specific precursor behaviors, such as shivering or forelimb grooming, whereas in other cases, these precursors are absent. These findings suggest that mice, like humans, exhibit characteristic itch-related behaviors. In the present study, we focused on interleukin-31 (IL-31), which has been implicated in atopic dermatitis-associated itch, and investigated whether precursor behaviors were observed during IL-31-induced itch-related behaviors in mice. Male ICR mice were used in this study. Following intradermal injection of IL-31, subsequent behaviors were recorded with a digital video camera, and scratch behaviors were counted based on the presence or absence of precursor behaviors. Intradermal IL-31-induced scratching with precursor behaviors was significantly higher than that without them. Dopamine D2 receptor agonists are reported to be effective against restless sensations. Ropinirole, a dopamine D2/D3 receptor agonist, significantly suppressed IL-31-induced scratching with precursor behaviors. Interestingly, ropinirole also attenuated IL-31-induced scratching without precursor behaviors. Histamine induces scratching that is unaccompanied by precursor behaviors compared to those accompanied by them. Ropinirole also inhibited histamine-induced scratching, both with and without precursor behaviors. In conclusion, these findings provide the first evidence that IL-31-induced itch-related responses are primarily characterized by precursor behaviors. Moreover, the fact that ropinirole significantly suppressed both IL-31- and histamine-induced scratching suggests that ropinirole holds therapeutic promise for managing diverse itch signaling pathways.

title: Exosome-Like Nanoparticles Derived from the Rhizome of Zingiber officinale Suppress Neuroinflammatory Responses in BV-2 Microglial Cells.
abstract: Plant-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (ELNs) are promising bioactive nanovesicles that can modulate physiological functions across species boundaries. Although ELNs derived from fresh plants have been extensively investigated, little is known about ELNs present in hot-water extracts used in traditional herbal medicines. We aimed to isolate and characterize ELNs derived from a hot-water extract of the rhizome of Zingiber officinale (Z-ELNs) and to evaluate their anti-neuroinflammatory effects in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated BV-2 microglial cells. Z-ELNs were isolated from ginger decoctions by differential ultracentrifugation and characterized using dynamic light scattering and transmission electron microscopy. The nanoparticles exhibited a mean diameter of 183 ± 56 nm and a zeta potential of -24.8 ± 12.1 mV. RNA sequencing analysis identified several known and putative microRNAs, while LC/MS analysis detected characteristic ginger-derived secondary metabolites, including 6-gingerol and 6-shogaol. Confocal microscopy demonstrated the uptake of fluorescently labeled Z-ELNs by BV-2 cells. The Z-ELN preparation significantly suppressed LPS-induced nitric oxide (NO) production and reduced the expression of inflammatory mediators, including inducible NO synthase, tumor necrosis factor-α, and interleukin-1β. Z-ELNs significantly upregulated heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) expression in BV-2 cells. These findings suggest that the Z-ELN preparation attenuates microglial inflammatory responses through multiple potential mechanisms, with HO-1 induction possibly being associated with these effects. Z-ELNs present in herbal decoctions may contribute to the pharmacological effects of traditional herbal medicines and warrant further investigation as potential sources of bioactive components targeting neuroinflammation.

title: Cortical Motor Hierarchy Disruption Is Associated With Functional Status in Early Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
journal: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neuromuscular disease characterised by progressive muscle wasting and functional decline. Although cortical motor network disruption is a hallmark of ALS, the large-scale functional hierarchy alterations and their underlying molecular mechanisms in the early stage of the disease (ALS-ES) remain poorly understood. We aimed to characterise cortical gradient changes in early-stage ALS and to examine their neurochemical and transcriptomic correlates, as well as their cross-sectional associations with clinical functional status. We recruited 97 patients with early-stage ALS, all at King's stage 1 and 94 healthy controls with comparable age and sex distributions. The ALS-ES group included 65 women and had a median ALSFRS-R score of 40 (IQR, 37-44). Resting-state fMRI was used to construct the principal functional gradient. We integrated neurochemical maps of 19 neurotransmitter receptors/transporters, and transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas. Partial least squares (PLS) regression and cell-type enrichment analysis were employed to identify molecular correlates of gradient alterations. Compared with HCs, ALS-ES patients exhibited a significant spatial contraction of the principal gradient. Specifically, gradient values significantly increased in the somatomotor network (SMN; t = 3.670, pFDR = 0.001) and decreased in the default mode network (DMN; t = -4.124, pFDR < 0.001). Within the ALS-ES group, higher SMN gradient values were associated with lower ALSFRS-R scores, whereas higher DMN gradient values were associated with higher ALSFRS-R scores. These macroscale alterations showed spatial correspondence with normative 5-HT4 receptor and norepinephrine transporter maps. PLS analysis identified a primary gene set (PLS1+) enriched in oligodendrocytes and mitochondrial functions (pFDR < 0.05), whereas the negative set (PLS1-) was associated with astrocytes, GABAergic neurons and RNA splicing pathways. Chromosome-level analysis revealed significant enrichment of PLS1- genes on chromosomes 5 and 16 (p < 0.05). Early-stage ALS is characterised by a collapsed cortical functional hierarchy centred on the motor-somatosensory axis. These alterations were spatially associated with normative neurochemical maps and distinct transcriptomic annotations related to energy metabolism and RNA processing. These findings identify cross-sectional cortical functional-hierarchy alterations associated with functional status in early-stage ALS and provide a multi-scale framework for investigating their neurochemical and transcriptomic correlates.

title: Swedish Consensus Recommendation for Follow-Up After ICU Stay.
abstract: A substantial proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) survivors experience long-term physical, psychological and cognitive impairments after critical illness. However, methods for identifying patients in need of post-ICU support vary widely. As a result, many patients are left without access to established rehabilitation pathways. This consensus recommendation provides a framework for the organisation and content of follow-up for adult ICU survivors in Sweden, informed by available evidence, stakeholder perspectives and expert consensus. The National System for Knowledge-Driven Healthcare Management (NPO) in Sweden commissioned the development of a practice recommendation for the follow-up of critically ill adults. Multidisciplinary experts in ICU survivorship formed a task force group. A systematic literature search in four databases was conducted in 2024 to identify pre-existing systematic reviews on the topic. The literature was reviewed, assessed for quality and recommendations were developed based on the literature evidence. The draft was discussed among multiprofessional groups involved in follow-up, in workshops with critical care nurses (n = 30) and professionals responsible for follow-up clinics (n = 74) and among patient representatives (n = 4). The final draft underwent external peer review by representatives from relevant professional organisations, the national registry for intensive care and governmental agencies in Sweden. The consensus recommendation suggests that all adult patients with an ICU length of stay ≥ 48 h are recommended for follow-up, with an initial contact within 1 week of ICU discharge to assess clinical status, identify early problems and ensure continuity of care. Patients and their families are recommended to be offered an outpatient follow-up visit at 2-3 months after discharge, led by ICU clinicians and, when possible, delivered by a multidisciplinary team. Validated screening tools and objective tests are recommended to assess relevant outcomes, including post-traumatic stress, anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment, physical function and Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) as appropriate. Patients with identified problems should be referred to appropriate healthcare providers or specialist services for further management. This consensus recommendation provides a framework for patient selection, timing and assessment to support a more structured and equitable management of post-intensive care syndrome. Systematic follow up of ICU survivors after hospital discharge is needed in order to assess long-term patient-centred outcomes. This is a consensus set of recommendations and not a GRADE-based clinical practice guideline for doing this, which can be considered by relevant ICUs.

title: Releasing the breaks: BK channels, sex differences and the paradox of CO2-induced calm.
Attenuated motor neuroplasticity after tongue-muscle training in older adults: A proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Low tongue pressure contributes to dysphagia by compromising safe swallowing. While tongue-lift training consistently induces corticomotor plasticity in younger individuals, neuromuscular efficacy and motor neuroplasticity in older adults remain unclear. This proof-of-concept study aimed to investigate central and peripheral motor adaptations following brief tongue-lift training in older adults with low tongue pressure. Thirteen older adults (8 women, mean age ± SD: 81 ± 4 years) with low tongue pressure (<30 kPa) underwent 41-minute standardized daily tongue-lift training over 5 consecutive days. Maximal tongue pressure was measured daily pre- and post-training. Transcranial magnetic stimulation was administered on days 1 and 5 to evaluate the resting motor threshold (MT) and motor-evoked potential (MEP) map areas of the tongue as measures of corticomotor excitability. Friedman tests were conducted to examine effects of time on outcome parameters. The 5-day tongue training induced a significant increase in maximal tongue pressure (33.0%; P = 0.005) with a significant decrease in its coefficient of variation (-51.5%, P = 0.030), accompanied by a significant decrease in the tongue MT (-11.3%, P < 0.001). However, the tongue MEP cortical map area did not change significantly (P = 0.853). These findings provide preliminary evidence for attenuated motor neuroplasticity following tongue-muscle training in older adults. Nevertheless, improved tongue motor function and corticobulbar excitability indicate that the potential for neurophysiological and functional adaptation remains intact. A better understanding of these age-related differences may contribute to the development of rehabilitation strategies for older adults with oral hypofunction.

title: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Strategies for Central and Peripheral Remyelination.
abstract: Myelin sheaths are produced by myelinating glia and provide metabolic support to neuronal axons while accelerating electrical signal conduction. Myelinating glia, which include oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system (CNS) and Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system (PNS), have distinct developmental origins and biological characteristics that profoundly influence their capacity for myelin regeneration following demyelinating insults. In various demyelinating diseases, loss of myelin and myelinating glia resulting from autoimmune disorders, inflammation, or genetic defects causes neurological dysfunction. Beyond removing disease-causing factors, inducing and accelerating remyelination represents a critical therapeutic goal for demyelinating diseases. In this review, we first summarize and compare molecular mechanisms underlying CNS and PNS remyelination, including extracellular signaling pathways, transcriptional regulation, and intercellular communication. We then highlight current treatments and ongoing clinical trials for common demyelination disorders, including neonatal white matter injury, multiple sclerosis, and inherited peripheral neuropathies.

title: Global synchrony moderates sad mood and is associated with emotional Stroop interference and somatic symptoms.
abstract: Mood-congruent attention in depression has been studied via emotional interference tasks, including tasks comparing responses to sad and happy stimuli. Mood induction offers a way to experimentally induce sad mood in non-clinical samples and examine its association with subsequent emotional interference, including Sad-Happy interference. Previous studies have separately linked resting-state global neural dynamics (synchrony, metastability) to depressive symptoms and attentional processing. However, whether individual differences in baseline global synchrony and metastability relate to how individuals respond to sad mood remains largely unclear. This study therefore examined the relationship between neural dynamics, sadder mood after induction, and Sad-Happy interference. Depressive symptoms also encompass somatic domains alongside cognitive-affective domains, though these are rarely distinguished in neuroimaging studies. We further examined whether baseline neural dynamics and their association with sadder mood and Sad-Happy interference were related to depressive symptoms (total, cognitive-affective, and somatic). Forty-eight non-clinical individuals completed resting-state neuroimaging, mood induction (sad or non-sad), and an emotional Stroop task. We found in a cross-sectional moderated mediation model that sadder mood after induction was associated with greater interference from sad compared to happy stimuli at medium and high levels of global synchrony, particularly in exploratory path models that included somatic symptoms. Findings suggest that individual differences in resting-state global synchrony may be a neural correlate of sadder mood after induction and Sad-Happy interference in non-clinical individuals. This study offers preliminary associations linking neural dynamics, sad mood, emotional interference, and somatic symptoms, providing insights into the role of neural dynamics in emotional and attentional processing.

title: Paraganglioma and childhood-onset optic atrophy in a SDHA compound heterozygous patient: an example of dual dominant and recessive inheritance.
abstract: SDHA pathogenic variants cause moderate to severe complex II deficiency, which manifests as a mitochondrial disorder in a homozygous/compound heterozygous child, or as hereditary cancer, mostly paraganglioma or pheochromocytoma, in a heterozygous adult. Here, we report the first composite heterozygous SDHA patient (hypomorphic allele p.(Thr508Ile) × null allele p.(Arg451His)) who developed complete congenital optic atrophy and a paraganglioma at the age of 36 yrs. No other germline variants were identified by sequencing panels of genes involved in these two disorders. This raises the question of whether paraganglioma screening should be implemented for carriers of a null SDHA variant.

title: Calsyntenin-2 promotes the pathology of acute myeloid leukemia via activation of the JAK2-STAT3 signaling pathway.
abstract: Although considerable progress has been made in the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), therapeutic outcomes remain unsatisfactory. Thus, it is of great important to investigate the leukemiagenesis mechanism of AML. Previous studies indicated that Calsyntenin-2 (CLSTN2) was closely associated with the progression of AML, however, roles and mechanisms of CLSTN2 in the pathology of AML remain unclear. In this study, series of methods including gene overexpression and knockdown, RT-qPCR, Western blot, CCK-8 assay, flow cytometry, colony formation assay, and RNA-sequencing was used to investigate roles and mechanisms of CLSTN2 in the biological behaviors of AML cell lines both in the in vivo and invitro experiments levels. CLSTN2 was high expressed in AML and predicts a poor prognosis. Knockdown the expression of CLSTN2 inhibited AML cell viability and clonogenic capacity, induced cell apoptosis, and caused G0/G1 phase arrest, whereas CLSTN2 overexpression displayed opposite results. Moreover, knockdown CLSTN2 reduced AML cells' infiltration, delayed disease progression, and prolonged the survival of xenograft mice, while CLSTN2 overexpression showed opposite results. MLL-AF9 induced AML mouse models results also verfied that CLSTN2 knockout inhibited the progression of AML. Mechanistically, CLSTN2 interacted with STAT3 and activated JAK2-STAT3 pathway to promote the pathology of AML, the STAT3 degrader SD-36 treatment could partially reverse CLSTN2 overexpression caused cell cycle acceleration, enhanced cell viability, colony formation ability and anti-apoptotic phenotype. CLSTN2 promoted cell proliferation, inhibited cell apoptosis, and accelerated the pathology of AML by interacting with STAT3 which led to the hyper-activation of JAK2-STAT3 signaling pathway. These results suggested that CLSTN2 might be a potential therapeutic target for AML.

title: Chitosan-coated vesicles in thermosensitive gel as a compelling platform for cannabidiol treatment of ocular disorders.
abstract: Topical ocular delivery of cannabidiol (CBD), a well-known phytocannabinoid with anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties, remains challenging because of its poor aqueous solubility, limited bioavailability, and rapid precorneal clearance. Nanocarrier-based and thermoresponsive mucoadhesive systems have emerged as promising approaches to overcome these limitations. We developed an advanced ocular delivery platform, consisting of CBD-loaded nanovesicles coated with chitosan (CS) embedded in a thermosensitive poloxamer-based in situ gel (Tg-CS-VS). Due to its positive charge and mucoadhesive properties, CS interacts with the negatively charged mucins of the tear film, prolonging residence time, promoting close contact with the corneal epithelium and transiently modulating tight junctions. These combined mechanisms markedly enhance the epithelial uptake and bioavailability of poorly soluble drugs such as CBD. A multivariate DoE approach optimized critical formulation parameters, including CS and poloxamer 407 concentrations and process variables. Tg-CS-VS exhibited nanovesicles with a mean diameter of of 176.5 ± 6.3 nm, polydispersity index of 0.215 ± 0.022 and ζ-potential of +24.0 ± 2.4 mV and suitable handling and rheological properties. CBD recovery was 98.3 ± 0.5% and gelation time was 15 s at corneal surface temperature. Mucin binding assays evidenced strong CS-mediated electrostatic interactions, supporting mucoadhesion. Good tolerability of the formulation was evidenced in corneal keratocytes cell line. In vivo studies in normotensive and transiently hypertensive rabbits showed excellent ocular tolerability and significant intraocular pressure (IOP) reduction, with maximal effect observed at 60 min post-administration. Overall, the formulation represents a highly promising, biocompatible system for anterior segment delivery of CBD, achieving efficient encapsulation, prolonged ocular residence and notable IOP-lowering activity. Further studies will explore its long-term therapeutic potential in chronic disease models.

title: The dual role of BDNF in epilepsy: insights from calpain-mediated TrkB-FL cleavage.
abstract: Despite the efficacy of current antiseizure medications in managing seizures, approximately one-third of patients develop refractory epilepsy, highlighting an urgent need to uncover the molecular mechanisms driving epileptogenesis. This process emerges from a complex interplay of molecular alterations, involving changes in neuronal signaling pathways. Among these, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its high-affinity receptor, the full-length tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB-FL), are heavily implicated in epilepsy pathophysiology. While traditionally recognized for promoting synaptic plasticity, BDNF signaling can become maladaptive in pathological states. Consequently, BDNF exhibits a paradoxical dual role in epilepsy, acting as a proepileptogenic factor in the acute phase, while exerting antiepileptic effects during the chronic phase. Recently, a calpain-dependent proteolytic mechanism mediating TrkB-FL cleavage, previously described in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and cerebral ischemia, has been shown to occur during epileptogenesis. Elevated levels of the intracellular cleavage product of TrkB-FL, TrkB-ICD, have been observed in the hippocampus of patients with refractory epilepsy, establishing its clinical relevance. In vitro, TrkB-ICD overexpression depolarizes neuronal membranes, increases miniature excitatory postsynaptic current frequency, and alters the transcription of genes related to synaptic transmission and plasticity. In vivo, its overexpression induces long-term memory impairment, a common comorbidity in epilepsy. Moreover, in experimental epilepsy models, TrkB-ICD protein levels correlate with seizure frequency during the acute phase (status epilepticus) and remain elevated during the chronic phase (established epilepsy). These findings highlight TrkB-FL cleavage and TrkB-ICD formation as molecular determinants in epileptogenesis, providing a biological rationale for the contrasting effects of BDNF. Inhibiting this cleavage, using tools like cell-penetrating peptides, represents a promising therapeutic avenue. As the field moves forward, elucidating the precise functions, regulation, and translational potential of the TrkB-FL proteolysis and TrkB-ICD formation may yield innovative, disease-modifying strategies for epilepsy, moving beyond the symptomatic suppression offered by conventional antiseizure drugs.

title: The Canadian underage substance use prevention (CUSP) trial: Amended protocol for a hybrid effectiveness-implementation cluster randomized trial of PreVenture.
abstract: Adolescent substance use remains a significant public health concern, particularly among youth with elevated personality-based risk profiles. PreVenture is a brief, personality-targeted intervention shown to reduce substance-related behaviours in prior randomized trials. The Canadian Underage Substance Use Prevention (CUSP) trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness and implementation of PreVenture under routine school conditions. CUSP is a three-arm, parallel-group, hybrid effectiveness-implementation cluster randomized controlled trial in public secondary schools across three Canadian provinces. Schools were randomized to: (1) PreVenture via a Train-the-Trainer model; (2) PreVenture Train-the-Trainer plus Implementation Facilitation; or (3) treatment-as-usual control. Grade 10 students completed baseline screening using the Substance Use Risk Profile Scale (SURPS); those scoring above predefined SURPS thresholds were invited to participate in PreVenture workshops and included in primary analyses. The primary outcome is screening positive for substance-related problems (CRAFFT score ≥ 2). Secondary outcomes include binge drinking, cannabis, illicit drug, and non-medical prescription drug use. Implementation outcomes include fidelity, reach, uptake, acceptability, and sustainability. Data collection is complete, but outcome analyses have not yet been conducted. The trial was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic and other implementation challenges, resulting in substantial attrition at both the student and school levels. This protocol documents modifications to the design and analytic plan, also reflected in the updated trial registration (NCT04198974), to ensure transparent reporting of findings. The pre-specified Statistical Analysis Plan, provided as an online supplement, was finalized and accepted by the trial steering committee prior to unblinding. NCT04198974.

title: Spatiotemporal Changes in the Cytokine Profile in the Brain of A53T Transgenic Mice, a Model of Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Neuroinflammation plays an important role in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease (PD), a widespread chronic neurodegenerative disorder. However, the dynamics of cytokine alterations in the brain during disease progression remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the levels of pro-inflammatory (IL-6, IL-17A, and IFN-γ) and anti-inflammatory (IL-4 and IL-10) cytokines in selected brain regions of transgenic A53T mice that express a mutant form of human α-synuclein and develop age-dependent pathological and behavioral abnormalities (a widely used model of PD). In young A53T mice (2- and 5-month-old), reduced emotionality was accompanied by elevated levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-17A in the striatum compared with age-matched control mice. In contrast, 10-month-old A53T mice exhibiting motor impairments showed reduced levels of IL-6, IFN-γ, and IL-4 in the striatum, together with increased IL-10 levels in the frontal cortex. Thus, age-dependent behavioral abnormalities in A53T mice were associated with distinct changes in the content of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines. The levels of all cytokines examined were altered in the striatum, whereas only IL-10 was significantly changed in the frontal cortex. No differences between A53T and control mice were detected in cytokine levels in the hippocampus. The observed spatiotemporal patterns of immune and inflammatory alterations may contribute to a better understanding of neuroinflammatory mechanisms underlying PD progression and may provide a basis for identifying potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: Role of Bach1 Transcription Factor in the Mechanisms of Cell Death.
abstract: Involvement of the transcription factor Bach1 in various scenarios of cellular regulation is reviewed herein. To date, the most extensively studied role of Bach1 is that of a repressor of the antioxidant genetic program initiated by the Nrf2 factor. This program counteracts oxidative stress, which triggers both ferroptosis and the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. Bach1 functions unrelated to the suppression of the Nrf2 transcriptional activity have been studied only fragmentarily. Nevertheless, among these, one could distinguish functions that are specific to the particular forms of cell death. A major consequence of such Nrf2-independent effects is, in particular, direct induction of the expression of the glutathione-specific gamma-glutamylcyclotransferase 1 (CHAC1) by Bach1; this leads to glutathione degradation and inactivation of the glutathione peroxidase 4 - a central enzyme in the ferroptosis mechanism responsible for the reduction of lipid peroxides. Independently of Nrf2, Bach1 also represses expression of the mitochondrial electron transport chain genes and activates expression of the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 1 (PDK1) and hexokinase 2 (HK2), thereby shifting cells toward the glycolytic pathway and rendering them more resistant to apoptosis. Furthermore, Bach1 influences expression of the inflammasome genes and modulates pyroptosis. Bach1 also regulates expression of a number of metallothionein genes and influences control of cuproptosis via the regulation of the free intracellular copper levels. Finally, Bach1 could inhibit autophagy through multiple mechanisms. In essence, the role of Bach1 in many processes - with the exception of the Bach1/Nrf2 axis - remains far from fully elucidated, given that the number of identified target genes exceeds 12,000, and the majority of them are regulated indirectly through formation of the specific protein complexes, which often include epigenetic enzymes. Nevertheless, in the context of various diseases - ranging from neurodegeneration to cancer - inhibition of Bach1 is precisely what is required to achieve a therapeutic effect. The review concludes by discussing clinical significance of Bach1 and the prospects for its therapeutic targeting.

title: When the Brain Signals Danger: Roles of Calreticulin and HMGB1 in Cell Death Mechanisms in Neurooncology and Neurodegeneration.
abstract: Contrary to the classical paradigm of brain immune privilege, damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) act as key mediators in the dialogue between CNS cells and the immune system, determining pathways of immune response development. This review examines the role of key DAMPs - calreticulin (CRT) and high-mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1) - in the functioning of CNS under normal conditions and during the development of neuropathologies, particularly oncological and neurodegenerative processes. Under normal conditions, CRT and HMGB1 ensure functioning of the brain, acting as necessary effectors of neurogenesis and homeostatic plasticity. In neurooncology, exposure of CRT on the surface of dying cells and release of HMGB1 serve as powerful adjuvant signals for antigen-presenting cells, inducing immunogenic cell death (ICD). Particular attention is given to the mechanisms of passive HMGB1 release during various types of regulated cell death (apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, cuproptosis), as well as to the role of redox modifications of the protein, which determine its pro-inflammatory, immunogenic, or tolerogenic properties. In neurodegeneration (Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), excessive DAMP release exacerbates the development of chronic neuroinflammation, disrupts integrity of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and forms a vicious cycle of pathological changes. Detection of CRT and HMGB1 in biological fluids or brain tissues has important prognostic potential, and regulation of their signaling pathways opens promising approaches for overcoming tumor resistance or inhibiting progressive neurodegenerative changes in the brain.

title: Mitochondria, Cell Death, and Neurodegeneration.
abstract: Mitochondria, acquired during the evolution of eukaryotic cells, have become essential organelles for cellular life. Beyond their well-established role in energy production, mitochondria are key regulators of intracellular signaling, acting as modulators of Ca2+ transport and major sources of reactive oxygen species. Mitochondrial metabolism is also closely linked to the metabolism of signaling molecules, including glutamate and monoamines. Another vital role of mitochondria is their involvement in the regulation of cell death. Disruption of mitochondrial functions contributes to the development of multiple pathological conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases. Here, we discuss how impairments in major mitochondrial processes contribute to neuronal death in neurodegenerative diseases and highlight the principal mitochondrial targets with potential pharmacological relevance.

title: Glial lipid reprogramming in brain aging: Lipid identity, organelle stress, and redox vulnerability.
abstract: Brain aging is accompanied by progressive glial dysfunction, impaired metabolic adaptation, oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to neurodegenerative disease. Although many studies of lipid metabolism in aging and neurodegeneration emphasize lipid abundance, lipid amount alone cannot explain why glia become redox-vulnerable. This review advances a chemistry-resolved integrative framework in which glial lipid reprogramming is understood through aging- and disease-associated changes in lipid identity, composition, oxidation state, storage form, subcellular localization, and lipid-mediated signaling. We discuss evidence from aged brain tissue, human neurodegenerative disease, iPSC-derived glial systems, and mouse models showing that altered lipid handling in microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells reshapes phagocytosis, inflammatory signaling, myelin processing, astrocytic metabolic support, and neuronal injury. We emphasize that acyl-chain saturation, head-group structure, oxidized lipid species, neutral lipid storage, plasmalogen-dependent redox buffering, peroxisomal lipid metabolism, and compartmental distribution determine how lipids regulate receptor engagement, lipid-droplet dynamics, lysosomal stress, mitochondrial function, ferroptotic susceptibility, and inflammatory redox signaling. Importantly, glial lipid reprogramming is further shaped by extracellular vesicle-mediated neuron-glia communication, regional lipid heterogeneity, and sex-dependent modifiers of glial metabolism. Oxidative stress therefore reflects the convergence of polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)-enriched membranes, oxidized phospholipids, oxysterols, ceramide accumulation, plasmalogen loss, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, lysosomal iron release, peroxisomal dysfunction, and declining glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), GTP cyclohydrolase 1-tetrahydrobiopterin (GCH1-BH4), and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-dependent protective systems. Finally, we discuss lipid-centered therapeutic opportunities targeting cholesterol efflux, apolipoprotein E (APOE) lipidation, lipid-droplet metabolism, sphingolipid pathways, lipid peroxide defense, plasmalogen support, extracellular vesicle biology, and lipid-based delivery systems. By shifting the focus from lipid accumulation to lipid identity, compartmental handling, and biological context, this review synthesizes glial lipid reprogramming as an integrative framework linking brain aging to redox-sensitive neurodegeneration.

title: Puberty, not age, marks the start of adolescent brain structural remodeling.
abstract: Many studies have shown that pubertal changes are associated with brain changes, but there lacks a clear understanding of what happens to the brain at puberty, and whether it opens the brain structural remodeling that characterizes adolescence. In this study, we used three longitudinal waves of structural MRI data from thousands of participants of the ABCD study aged 9-14 years to compare brain changes between age-matched children who had either reached or not reached a major pubertal milestone: menarche in females and fonarche (voice drop) in males. We found that only the children who had reached the milestone exhibited widespread contraction of cortical surface area and subcortical volume. The contraction was more pronounced in females, in line with previous evidence of how gonadal hormones regulate neuronal fine-tuning. Our findings suggest that reaching puberty, rather than reaching a particular age, begins the adolescent phase of structural brain development.

title: Reply to the Editor "Endovascular therapy for mild-to-moderate stroke due to basilar artery occlusion: Interpreting the certainty of excellent functional recovery".
Non-invasive skin trace elementomics reveals a characteristic pattern of essential element deficiency and toxic element accumulation in children with ADHD.
journal: Biometals : an international journal on the role of metal ions in biology, biochemistry, and medicine
abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is the most common neurodevelopmental disorder in childhood. Its clinical diagnosis primarily relies on behavioral assessments, lacking objective and non-invasive biological indicators. Trace elements are involved in neurotransmitter synthesis, myelin development, and prefrontal cortex function regulation, and their imbalance may be associated with the pathogenesis of ADHD. However, previous studies have mostly focused on single elements, lacking systematic evidence at the omics level. To analyze the differences in 30 skin element levels between children with ADHD and healthy controls, and to explore the associations of elemental imbalances with core symptoms, anxiety, and executive function, thereby providing a basis for non-invasive screening of childhood ADHD.
